title: No regret here
hookLine: a hospice nurse, Bronnie Ware, reported common regrets: living for others' expectations, working too much

cards: Long afternoons at a bedside. The talk turns, as it sometimes does, to what a person wishes they had done differently.

A woman named Bronnie Ware, who took work caring for people near the end of their lives, in their own homes, listened. Later she wrote it down: first as a short piece online, then as a book. It isn't a study.
Nobody counted anything. It's one carer's notebook of what she heard at the bedside. But its sentences are plain enough to stop a person in the middle of an ordinary week.

teach.b: First, what she heard. In Ware's telling, people wished they had found the courage to live a life true to themselves, not the life others expected of them. They wished they hadn't worked so hard.
Others wished they had said what they felt, kept up with old friends, or let themselves be happier.

teach.h: REGRETS OF WHAT WAS LEFT UNDONE
teach.b: Second, notice what kind of regrets these are. Not disasters or headlines. Things left undone, quietly, a day at a time: the call not made, the evening given to the office again, the honest sentence swallowed.
Third, an older voice saying something close.

Henry David Thoreau went to live in a small cabin by Walden Pond, and in his book Walden he explained why: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived."
He wasn't dying. He wanted the dying person's clarity early. Fourth, a fair warning about the source.
Ware presents this as what she heard, not as research, and memory and the listener both shape a story.
So it works best as a mirror, not a rule. If one regret catches, look at the timing: every one on her list points at something a living person can still change.
No regret here. Not everywhere. Just here, in one place you choose.

how: Some people reread a short list of end-of-life regrets, such as Bronnie Ware's, and choose one concrete change to make while there is time, sometimes alongside a journal or a conversation with someone close.

games.why: today's practice: one change, chosen and made. every regret on Ware's list points at something a living person can still change.

practice: Go through her list slowly, one at a time: others' expectations, too much work, feelings unsaid, friends who drifted, happiness put off until later, and notice whether one of them catches.

You don't need to fix a whole life; just let one small change come to mind, a phone call, leaving on time one evening, one honest sentence to someone who should hear it. Hold that one change, and let the rest go.

wordCard.voice: Bronnie Ware, the carer whose bedside notebook of regrets became a book about living true to yourself. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: front only the essential facts. One small change is enough. See you tomorrow.
